The design of such circuit is difficult due to the lack of cryogenic transistor models from the foundries. Both simulations and experimental results are shown. The proposed circuit is characterized with particular focus on energy resolution, linearity, bandwidth and power consumption. Specifically, a 1.08 keV resolution was measured on the test bench simulating the detector with a 15 pF ceramic capacitor and filtering the signals with a quasi-Gaussian shaping amplifier. Circuit linearity is compliant with gamma spectroscopy requirements. The preamplifier is also equipped with an innovative solution that allows for high-resolution spectroscopy in an energy range that exceeds the natural saturation limit of the circuit and, at the same time, reduces dramatically the dead-time in case of high-energy events inside the crystals due to heavy ions or cosmic rays. For events of energy greater than 15 MeV, a resolution, expressed as FWHM, better than 0.11% was measured.

articleTitle: Multimodal HYPR-based Denoising for Improving Brain Pattern Analysis
publicationTitle: 2022 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium and Medical Imaging Conference (NSS/MIC)
abstract: Brain pattern analysis is an exploratory yet powerful method for deriving disease-related patterns that function as imaging biomarkers. Given that multiple functional systems may be affected in disease, pattern analysis applied to multimodal imaging datasets provides an increasingly detailed view of pathophysiology. Voxelwise pattern analysis is a purely data-driven method for identifying which regions of the brain are most affected. Given the high voxel noise in these datasets, aggressive spatial filtering is usually employed before analysis. However, it has yet to be investigated whether more sophisticated, resolution-preserving denoising operators, such as HYPR, can improve the precision, interpretability, and robustness of identified patterns. As a foray into these questions, we apply HYPR-based denoising to a small pilot FDG-PET/fMRI dataset of Parkinson’s disease subjects before applying pattern analysis. FDG data are reconstructed using PSF-HYPR4D-K-TOFOSEM and fMRI data are processed with a proposed novel 4D HYPR operator. PET denoising reduces noise-induced variation by up to 40% and HYPR-based fMRI denoising enables voxelwise joint analysis of the PET and fMRI data, allowing one to analyze patterns of accordance and discordance from the functional metrics of each modality. Applying voxelwise pattern analysis to the denoised dataset versus traditional aggressive spatial filtering minimizes the amount of resolution loss, allowing for subregional pattern structure to be more precisely characterized. Therefore, more sophisticated denoising provides truly voxelwise, more interpretable patterns, which may have downstream effects on disease understanding and treatment.

articleTitle: A Self-supervised Learning Method for Denoising Dynamic PET Images from List-mode Data
publicationTitle: 2022 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium and Medical Imaging Conference (NSS/MIC)
abstract: Dynamic positron emission tomography (PET) imaging usually suffers from a low signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) due to limited counts in each frame acquired in a short period of time. In order to denoise dynamic PET images, this paper proposes a self-supervised deep learning method in the list-mode data domain. We design a random sampling process to divide data collected along lines of response (LORs) into two groups to reconstruct training image pairs in each iteration. Then the network takes the training image as the input and outputs the denoised image. A simulation study shows that our method performs better in suppressing noise and retaining details than the traditional iterative method followed by denoising filters and the self-supervised denoising method in the image domain.

articleTitle: Bias and Temperature Effects on DCR and RTS Fluctuations in 1- and 2-Layer CMOS SPADs
publicationTitle: 2022 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium and Medical Imaging Conference (NSS/MIC)
abstract: Single photon avalanche diodes (SPADs) fabricated in a 150 nm CMOS technology are characterized under different bias and temperature conditions. The device under test consists of a chip including arrays of SPADs with different active area and different avalanche quenching network, either passive or active. Both single-layer and dual-layer SPAD array configurations (the latter being based on the face-to-face interconnection of two virtually identical chips) are investigated. Measurements are focused on breakdown voltage and dark count rate (DCR) performance, with particular emphasis on DCR fluctuations of the random telegraph signal (RTS) kind.

articleTitle: Synthetic Full Dose Cardiac PET Images from Low Dose Scans Using Conditional GANs
publicationTitle: 2022 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium and Medical Imaging Conference (NSS/MIC)
abstract: Positron emission tomography (PET) is often used to characterize diagnosing cancer, heart diseases, and neurological disorders. Radiation exposure to patients results from the injection of radioactive tracers. Researchers have proposed deploying various artificial intelligence (AI) methods to enhance image quality while reducing radiation dose. Lowering the dose, however, will result in low signal-to-noise-ratio (SNR) and loss of information, thus leading to difficulties with clinical decision making. To address this problem, we evaluated the performance and generalizability of a deep-learning algorithm for improving the quality and accuracy of low dose cardiac PET image quality. Our model structure is based on a conditional generative adversarial neural network (cGAN) including a U-net generator with skip connections and a discriminator. Model training and validations were performed on a low dose PET dataset simulated from a full dose dataset acquired from 40 patient. Low dose cardiac 18F-fluorodeoxyglucose (<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">18</sup>F-FDG) PET scans were reconstructed using reduced PET raw data by randomly selecting 5 to 14% of the total events in the PET list mode data. We demonstrate through quantification that the cGAN framework successfully creates synthetic full dose images from low dose scans while preserving the original image resolution with significant noise correction.

articleTitle: HVCMOS Active Pixel Sensors for Measuring GCR and SEP
publicationTitle: 2022 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium and Medical Imaging Conference (NSS/MIC)
abstract: The development of depleted monolithic active pixel sensors to be used for the measurement of the tracks and the energy depositions of galactic cosmic ray and solar energetic particles is presented. Simulations and preliminary measurements verify the design choices. The chip comprises of the pixel array, an embedded controller, ADC, and bias circuits. In normal operation mode only hit pixels are readout. The technology used permits the placement of the CMOS devices in shallow n and p wells which are separated from the deep n-well by a buffer p-substrate. The sensing diode consists of a high resistivity p-type substrate biased at a negative voltage and the segmented deep n-well on its top. The dynamic range of energy depositions and of count rates to be handled spans many orders of magnitude. For this reason, two designs have been performed one with low gain tailored to high energy depositions and one with high gain for the low energy depositions.

articleTitle: DB-SPECT, a Fixed-Gantry SPECT Scanner for Dynamic Brain Imaging: Design Concept and First Results
publicationTitle: 2022 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium and Medical Imaging Conference (NSS/MIC)
abstract: Brain Single Photon Emission Computed Tomography (SPECT) imaging has seen renewed interest for clinical applications such as epilepsy, dementia, Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, and tumor imaging. In this work we show that our brain-dedicated SPECT scanner design can achieve high resolution and sensitivity by incorporating large detector coverage enabled by 118 detector modules where each module is comprised of 5x5x1 cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup> CsI:Tl scintillator coupled with an array of SiPMs. The DB-SPECT design is based on detectors with high intrinsic resolution detecting gamma-rays from a 210 mm dia. FOV through lofthole collimator. The reconstructed images show that at the same system sensitivity of the conventional dual head gamma camera (0.01%), calculated resolution is 4.05 mm FWHM while some of the 2 mm dia. and all of the 2.65 mm dia. hot rods in a Derenzo phantom are resolved. We further implemented a mixed collimator design where the 118 collimators are divided in to 4 groups with each group having different collimator dimension ranging from 0.5 to 2.0 mm. This resulted in high sensitivity thanks to the collimator groups with larger hole sizes and high resolution where the groups with small collimator hole contributed to recovered resolution. This mixed collimator design features 5.6x sensitivity gain compared to the dual head gamma camera while 2.65 mm dia. hot rods are partially resolved.

articleTitle: Improved Quality of 3-D Compton Images by List-Mode EMTV Reconstruction
publicationTitle: 2022 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium and Medical Imaging Conference (NSS/MIC)
abstract: The Compton camera does not require a collimator and can detect gamma rays in a wide energy range, so it is expected as a new nuclear medicine modality. The aim of this study is to improve the quality of three-dimensional (3-D) Compton images by reconstruction using total variation (TV) regularization. We incorporated TV regularization into the list-mode maximum likelihood expectation maximization (LM-MLEM) reconstruction method for 3-D Compton imaging. This is called list-mode expectation maximization total variation (LM-EMTV). A Monte Carlo simulation of a Compton camera was performed with a Cs-137 uniform plane source, projection data in 12 directions were acquired, and the image quality was evaluated by the uniformity and the edge blurring of the reconstructed image. We also examined the possibility of reducing the number of projections. From results of simulation, the uniformity of image reconstructed using LM-EMTV improved 66% without edge degradation. In addition, even if the number of projections reduced to directions, which is half of the 12 directions, an image with the same quality as that by the conventional MLEM method was obtained. In conclusion, LM-EMTV image reconstruction method improved the quality of the 3-D Compton images, suggesting the possibility of reducing the number of projections.

articleTitle: The Tile Rear Extension module for the ATLAS Level-1 Calorimeter Trigger Upgrade
publicationTitle: 2022 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium and Medical Imaging Conference (NSS/MIC)
abstract: For the Run-3 data-taking period at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC), the hardware-based Level-1 Calorimeter Trigger (L1Calo) of the ATLAS experiment is undertaking a major upgrade campaign. The upgrade introduces new feature extractor (FEX) processors running complex algorithms which will increase the trigger performance in a challenging high-pileup environment, while lowering the thresholds. In order to provide information from the ATLAS hadronic calorimeter to the trigger processors, new state-of-the-art FPGA-based Tile Rear Extension (TREX) modules have been developed, produced and installed for the existing L1Calo PreProcessor system which interface to the FEX modules via high-speed optical links operating at 11.2 Gbps. The path to the legacy trigger processors is maintained via electrical cables. The TREX modules format, pack and deliver digitized transverse energy results to the downstream modules in real-time at the rate of the LHC clock (40.08 MHz). To verify the trigger decision, the TREXs also format and transfer event data to the ATLAS DAQ system. The event data transfer is performed via optical links running at 9.6 Gbps to Front-End Link Exchange (FELIX) boards. The interface to the legacy readout path is preserved via a single optical link running at 800 Mbps in G-Link transmission mode to Readout Driver (ROD) boards. The monitoring and configuration of TREX on-board devices is carried out by a System-on-Chip (SoC). During the comissioning phase 32 modules have been installed and fully integrated within ATLAS. The modules show stable performance and are used during standard operation of the ATLAS detector.

articleTitle: Long-length Scintillating Fibers for Nuclear Waste Repositories
publicationTitle: 2022 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium and Medical Imaging Conference (NSS/MIC)
abstract: This paper describes the fabrication, testing, and characterization of long-length, up to 50 m, scintillating fibers for the purpose of radiation monitoring in inaccessible radiological and nuclear waste repositories. The fabrication aspect was focused on ruggedizing the 1-mm diameter fiber and limiting external light interference for fibers. Testing and characterization were performed in a laboratory setting with radiation sources, a photosensor module and a multi-channel analyzer. Light attenuation was studied as a function of distance by analyzing both the spectrum and count rate. Additionally, the scintillating fibers were coupled to optical communication fibers (100 m) to extend the reach of the system. This paper also includes the optical spectrometry results from the sensitivity and response of the signal attenuation. Lastly, the paper covers the field testing of the scintillating fibers in a relevant environment.

articleTitle: Quantitative CT-less PET Imaging in the Presence of Prior Attenuation Coefficient Distribution
publicationTitle: 2022 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium and Medical Imaging Conference (NSS/MIC)
abstract: In this study, we explore quantitative PET imaging without CT as a solution to true low-dose PET scan. The proposed reconstruction algorithm is particularly suitable when prior attenuation information, i.e. previous CT data, is available. Gaussian mixture models (GMM) were used to define the distribution of attenuation coefficients within the patient body using the prior CT data. Incorporating the background radiation from lutetium in LSO as ‘transmission data’ along with predefined GMM, a so-called TOF-MLAA-GMM was developed. In the proposed algorithm, attenuation maps from LSO background radiation are employed to provide information about non-radioactive objects in the FOV (such as patient bed), create suitable initial conditions and scatter data, and minimize the scaling problem in TOF-MLAA. A NEMA NU-2-like phantom and <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">18</sup>F-FDG patient data from a long-axial FOV scanner, Biograph Vision Quadra PET/CT (Siemens Healthineers), were used to evaluate the developed algorithm. For both the phantom and patient data, PET images from TOF-MLAA-GMM were compared against those from TOF-MLAA and OSEM using CT-based attenuation and scatter corrections. Studying both the phantom and patient PET images, it was seen that the developed TOF-MLAA-GMM algorithm outperforms TOF-MLAA. Analysis of the mean SUV across various organs of the patient showed a mean quantification error of -14.80% (range: -27.20 to -6.93%) in the PET images using TOF-MLAA and 10.64% (range: 2.20% to 14.55%) when using TOF-MLAA-GMM attenuation maps. The proposed method can therefore be used in low-dose PET studies where previous attenuation data are available to avoid repeated CT scans.

articleTitle: A Deep-learning Based Method to Generate Energy-Dependent System Matrices for a 4π View Gamma Imager
publicationTitle: 2022 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium and Medical Imaging Conference (NSS/MIC)
abstract: Radioactive sources are widely used in industrial and medical applications. Our lab has developed a collimator-free, high-sensitivity gamma camera to image radiation sources in a 4π FOV. In our approach, the measurement of system matrices for different radiation sources is essential for accurate imaging, which is time-consuming and inconvenient for realistic application. Therefore, it is significant to develop an efficient method to accomplish fast system matrix measurement among various kinds of radiation sources.Recently, deep learning methods have been demonstrated to be effective in image-to-image translation in nuclear medicine imaging. Inspired by this, we investigated the U-Net architecture to generate energy-dependent system matrices from 140 keV to 1333 keV. Monte Carlo simulations were performed to generate datasets. The detector response function (DRF) images were generated as the input and output for network training. The Normalized Root Mean Square Error (NMRSE) was calculated to evaluate the DRF prediction accuracy. Besides, single-source positioning bias was evaluated for image reconstruction accuracy. Results showed that U-Net-based methods can satisfactorily generate an energy-dependent system matrix and the absolute positioning bias of single point source reconstruction are smaller than 2° for both θ and φ directions. For the same system matrix generation task, e.g. <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">99m</sup>Tc, a Dual-Input strategy showed better performance than a Single-Input strategy.

articleTitle: Interpretable PET/CT Radiomic Based Prognosis Modeling of NSCLC Recurrent Following Complete Resection
publicationTitle: 2022 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium and Medical Imaging Conference (NSS/MIC)
abstract: This study aimed to develop an interpretable prognostic model with a nomogram for Non-Small Cell Lung Cancer (NSCLC) recurrence prediction following complete resection, using multi-modality PET/CT fusion radiomics and patients’ clinical features. Retrospectively, 181 NSCLC patients who had undergone <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">18</sup>F-FDG PET/CT scan were enrolled and split into training (2/3) and testing (1/3) partitions. Before image fusion, PET and CT images were registered, resized to equal isotropic voxel size, and clipped and normalized. Guided Filtering Fusion GFF algorithm was used for image fusion. Two hundred eighteen radiomic features were extracted from each PET, CT, and fused image, including morphological, first-order statistical, and texture features. Clinical features included age, sex, smoking status, weight, radiation, chemotherapy, pathological stage, etc. Feature selection and univariate and multivariate modeling were performed using the CoxBoost algorithm. Harrell’s Concordance index (C-index) was used to evaluate the performance of the models, and compare C test was used to statistically compare the performance of the models (p-values < 0.05 were considered significant). Clinical, Clinical+PET, Clinical+CT, and Clinical+GFF resulted in c-indices (confidence interval) of 0.701 (0.589-0.812), 0.757 (0.647-0.867), 0.706 (0.607, 0.807), and 0.824 (0.751-0.896), respectively. Statistical comparison of the performance of different models with the Clinical model revealed that while PET and GFF features can significantly increase the performance (p-values 0.009 and 0.001, respectively), CT features did not significantly improve the performance of the Clinical model (p-value 0.279). Therefore, the nomogram was developed based on the Clinical+GFF model (with the best performance). Radiomic features extracted from PET and PET/CT fusion images can improve the recurrence prognosis in NSCLC patients compared to the conventional clinical factors alone.

articleTitle: TOF Offset Monitoring and Correction of PET System Based on NEMA NEC Data
publicationTitle: 2022 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium and Medical Imaging Conference (NSS/MIC)
abstract: A method to monitor and correct crystal-level Time-of-Flight (TOF) offset error of Positron Emission Tomography system based on NEMA NEC phantom data is studied, which improves the accuracy of the TOF resolution measurement and reduces the dependence on time correction experiment. The method calculates the TOF offset error of each crystal with the time difference error of all true coincidence events, which are decided by removing scatter and random events following the TOF resolution test in NEMA NU2-2018. The time difference due to the physical position of line source is corrected. The centroid of the statistical distribution of the time difference error represents the residual error of TOF offset of each crystal, which acts as a criterion of time correction status of the crystal. For poorly corrected crystals, the TOF offset could be corrected by adding the residual part. To improve the stability of the correction performance, an iterative process is applied. This method is applied to both experiment and simulation NEC phantom data of uMI Panorama PET/CT system, where the poorly corrected crystal modules are successfully located and corrected, and the TOF resolution performance recovers after the corrections.

articleTitle: Study of ASIC Readout Used for Detectors in an MR Compatible, RF-Penetrable TOF-PET Insert
publicationTitle: 2022 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium and Medical Imaging Conference (NSS/MIC)
abstract: Developing positron emission tomography (PET) systems with high channel number has driven the need for application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs) owing to their compactness, multi-channel readout capability, and excellent time and energy resolution performance. They can also be quite flexible by employing field-programmable gate arrays (FPGAs) in the readout circuit. In particular, the ASIC+FPGA approach provides a high performance and compact solution for TOF-PET applications. ASICs serve functions of extracting time and energy information from analog SiPM signals, and an FPGA is employed for other application-specific requirements like on-board chip configuration, communication with data acquisition (DAQ) systems, and system monitoring. Based on this foundation, we developed TOF-capable detector modules for our second generation RF-penetrable PET insert. During our previous experiments, we found that different trigger and readout methods lead to different noise pattern and intensity in MR environment, and also have different singles count loss ratio. This paper aims to study and compare different readout configurations for our MR-compatible detectors. We studied four trigger and readout methods: hit-standard, frequent-standard, hit-bypass, and frequent-bypass, and compared their singles count loss ratios with both theoretical models and experimental results. For all four methods, the theoretical results matched the experimental results well. The two methods which used bypass mode performed better than those using the standard mode approach. With the most optimized trigger and readout method (hit-bypass), we achieved 1.2% singles count loss ratio at a 20 kcps count rate per channel.

articleTitle: Titanium Implants for Field Verification in Proton Therapy – an Applicability Test
publicationTitle: 2022 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium and Medical Imaging Conference (NSS/MIC)
abstract: Positron emission tomography (PET) for off-line field verification has been found limited by the so-called wash-out of the produced activity distribution due to biological transport processes. The activation of implants has been proposed to overcome this limitation and the general potential of titanium implants has been demonstrated in the past. Compared to implanted markers, titanium implants are used during surgical resection especially in brain tumor patients which is often performed prior to the radiotherapy treatment. An applicability test for the use of titanium implants for field verification is demonstrated. The test includes a phantom study with simple geometric phantoms and an anthropomorphic phantom. Furthermore, Monte-Carlo (MC) simulations are performed to predict the expected activity in the implants. The visual analysis reveals the general applicability for clinical implantation, while the numerical analysis of the results demonstrates the current limitations given by PET imaging and the basic physical knowledge of the activation cross sections. With the results, requirements for future generations of PET scanners for field verification in proton therapy can be derived. Necessary physics research on activation cross section can be deduced from the results. With further development in PET imaging, the incorporation of implant activation may provide an additional means for the monitoring of treatment delivery. On a qualitative basis, PET imaging of titanium implants may already be used in clinical practice for patients which come with suitable implants. Furthermore, possibly suitable implant positions can be derived from the results.

articleTitle: A Low Noise, Low Frequency Subsystem for Cryogenic Sensing
publicationTitle: 2022 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium and Medical Imaging Conference (NSS/MIC)
abstract: In this paper, the design of a warm electronics board to provide non-RF control and bias lines to a warm readout system for cryogenic microwave SQUID (superconducting quantum interface device) multiplexing is presented. That system, the SLAC Microresonator Radio Frequency (SMuRF) platform, is a next-generation control and readout system for superconducting microresonators which can be used for a variety of imaging applications ranging from x-rays to Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) experiments. Focus is given to circuits biasing the cryogenic Transition-Edge Sensors (TES), providing a flux ramp to align the sensor outputs, and circuits to provide software control of gate and drain biases of RF amplifiers in the SMuRF system. Techniques used to reduce the primary components of low frequency noise present in the SMuRF system will also be discussed.

articleTitle: First Animal Scan on C-SPECT
publicationTitle: 2022 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium and Medical Imaging Conference (NSS/MIC)
abstract: C-SPECT is designed for dynamic cardiac SPECT of human patients [1] - [4]. It is stationary during acquisition, but its collimation is adaptive through adjustable slat stacks for axial collimation and a selection of slits for transverse collimation. In this study, we performed our first animal scans with quantitative comparison of activity concentration with ex-vivo tissue samples. A 54-kg male Yorkshire swine was sedated, intubated and ventilated mechanically during the procedure, with monitoring throughout. The animal was positioned in the scanner, which was set to high-resolution mode. 21 mCi of <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">99m</sup>Tc-labeled sestamibi was injected intravenously just after the start of a 300-s acquisition. Five additional static scans were performed with a change of axial FOV for the last. The heart was excised, sectioned according to the 17-segment AHA model, weighed, and assayed to determine true activity concentration. The emission data were reconstructed using an ML-EM algorithm with resolution modeling. The reconstructions were reoriented into traditional cardiac views and concentrations were compared to tissue values. A second 65-kg make Yorkshire pig was imaged using the same procedure with a 22 mCi injection of <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">99m</sup>Tc-labeled sestamibi. For the first swine, the heart was partially truncated since the animal was positioned low relative to the FOV. Consequently, 10 of 17 segments were available for comparison. The second swine was positioned appropriately and good imaging quality was obtained. In conclusion, despite some positioning problems during the first scan, the overall success of that experiment suggested future experiments to test quantification of myocardial blood flow in comparison with microspheres were feasible. That second experiment with additional microsphere injection was conducted and resulted in good image quality.

articleTitle: High-Rate Handling Solution for Multiple Channels, FPGA-Based, Time-to-Digital Converters
publicationTitle: 2022 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium and Medical Imaging Conference (NSS/MIC)
abstract: With the increasing complexity of applications, the demand of high-counts number of channels for Time-to-Digital Converters (TDC) has grown, creating the issue of handling multiple timestamps contemporaneously. In this contribution, we will present the BeltBus (BB), a solution that is able to handle several TDC channels and can reach a measurement rate of several hundreds of Msps. Moreover, BeltBus temporally orders the incoming timestamps to reduce the computation effort of the following elaboration modules; e.g., time-taggers and histogrammers. Finally, the Beltbus allows to have an high dynamic range and an high resolution without having routing issues in the FPGA.Theese tasks are performed thanks to several cascaded IP-Cores(Node Inserters), which are responsible for the comparison of a TDC channel timestamp with the output from the previous node and for sending out the lowest one. This means that each node has 2 inputs and 1 outputs, except for the first one, which has only the input from the TDC. This architecture, with respect the calssical parallel one, allows to have a modular design suited to support a very high number of channels. Indeed, the BeltBus is capable of handling hundred of channels with overall data rate (DR) of several Msps at the state-of-the-art.The whole system has been tested on a 16 channels TDC made with an Artix-7 Field-Programmable Gate Array (FPGA) clockied at 100 MHz, wich has a resolution of 1 ps and a FullScale Range (FSR) of 10.3 s. With this setup an overall DR of 98.3 Msps has been obtained, obtaining a transmission efficiency of 98.3%.

articleTitle: Confidence Score Estimation in Machine Learning-based Automated Lesion Segmentation from PET Images
publicationTitle: 2022 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium and Medical Imaging Conference (NSS/MIC)
abstract: Despite the exceptional performance of the deep learning approaches, these techniques still produce non-negligible errors and/or outliers. Error prediction would be highly critical in sensitive applications such as medical image classification, segmentation, and outcome estimation. The focus of this work is on the means to provide a confidence score or certainty degree for a given task to warn the users when there are high risks of gross errors. Such certainty scores would be highly desirable for machine learning-based solutions in medicine to demand extra verification through human examination for cases with a low confidence score. To obtain a confidence score for lesion segmentation from PET images, in the first phase a deep learning model is trained to predict lesion masks in an end-to-end fashion from standard PET images (full-dose). The prediction of lesion mask is carried out using the standard PET images as well as a number of low-dose and/or noisy PET images with different noise levels. The same model trained on the standard PET data is employed to predict the lesion masks from the different noisy PET images. Due to the increased noise levels in the input PET images, certain levels of disagreement would be observed across the predicted lesion masks from standard and noisy PET images. The level of agreement (and/or disagreement) across the predicted lesion masks would indicate the confidence score for the given subject in the test (or inference) phase without knowing the ground truth mask. Intuitively, for easy cases, the model would not be challenged to discriminate the lesion from the background even in the presence of high noise levels. However, when the noise in the input PET images is increased, the model would be highly challenged to detect the lesion, particularly in difficult cases. The confidence scores generated by the proposed framework exhibited a good correlation with the Dice scores calculated using the ground truth data (y=1.05X + 0.8, R<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>=0.90). The confidence score reflects the accuracy of lesion segmentation from PET images. Given these confidence scores, users/clinicians would have a dependable measure that determines to what extent they can rely on the obtained results.

articleTitle: Improving Evaluations of Neutron Induced Gamma Ray Production: Upgrading ENDF, Formatting and Reaction Models
publicationTitle: 2022 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium and Medical Imaging Conference (NSS/MIC)
abstract: This paper describes part of the joint efforts of Brookhaven National Laboratory, Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, and Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory to revise the gamma production library in ENDF/B-VIII.0 modeling in transport codes under the Gamma Rays Induced by Neutrons (GRIN) project. Simulation modelling support and event-by-event calculations are addressed. The improvements enable a better modelling of particle-gamma and gamma-gamma coincidences and provide significant upgrades to the ENDF/B library, data format, and reaction models.

articleTitle: Performance of Large Area TSV SiPM Array on Fused Silica Tiles
publicationTitle: 2022 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium and Medical Imaging Conference (NSS/MIC)
abstract: Large silicon photomultiplier (SiPM) arrays are used to collect scintillation light in noble liquid detectors such as DarkSide, nEXO, MEGII, ProtoDUNE and DUNE. The requirement of strict radiopurity for some of these detectors necessitate the use of fused silica substrate as the carrier of through silicon via (TSV) SiPM arrays with through quartz via (TQV) for front to backside electrical connections. We characterize the photodetection of these SiPM arrays and demonstrate the single-photoelectron detection in cryogenic environments. The intrinsically larger capacitance (a few nF/cm<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sup>) of these SiPM arrays require a light readout concept by weakly couple the photoelectron signal to a charge sensitive amplifier. We will explore the performance on this light readout system using arrays of TSV SiPM tiles.

articleTitle: Effects of Random Coincidences on Image Quality for a Preclinical CZT PET System
publicationTitle: 2022 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium and Medical Imaging Conference (NSS/MIC)
abstract: When compared to the clinical state-of-the-art of PET, small animal imaging systems under perform in terms of spatial resolution performance when investigating identical organs such as the brain. To develop ultra-high resolution systems, semiconductor-based detectors are appealing compared to scintillators since the intrinsic resolution is achieved by the pitch of electrodes deposited on the crystal rather than requiring the cutting and processing of minuscule crystal rods. This work investigates the potential of cadmium zinc telluride as a PET detection material in a dual-panel system configuration. A resolution phantom study was performed where the phantom was rotated to four positions to overcome the limited angular sampling of the dual panel geometry. Normalization was performed using a cylinder of equivalent diameter. The preliminary reconstruction demonstrated the ability to visualize 2.4 mm rods in the phantom with only normalization correction implemented. Investigation of the random coincidence contributions to the prompt data showed very high randoms/true fractions ranging from 76% down to 67%, owing to poor coincidence time resolution in this preliminary study. The current data demonstrated the ability to perform PET imaging using semiconductor materials while also indicating the need for further corrections at both coincidence and singles levels to realize the potential of this PET system for preclinical imaging.

articleTitle: ECG-Gating to Aid Attenuation Map Alignment in Cardiac SPECT using Data Consistency Conditions
publicationTitle: 2022 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium and Medical Imaging Conference (NSS/MIC)
abstract: In Single Photon Emission Computed Tomography (SPECT), accurate attenuation correction requires alignment of emission data with an attenuation map. Data consistency conditions (DCCs) depend on attenuation and can thus be exploited to provide an alignment method. DCCs have been used previously for attenuation correction in PET and SPECT. DCCs exist for parallel-hole geometry but not for pinhole SPECT collimation, however, interpolation of pinhole projections into parallel-hole projections allows application of parallel-hole DCCs. The assumptions of the DCC approach require the activity to be contained within a contiguous convex region of constant attenuation. This is violated in cardiac imaging due to extra-cardiac activity in structures like the liver and the heterogeneity of the attenuation in thorax. We hypothesize that electrocardiogram (ECG)-gating can be used to separate dynamic activity in the heart from static background signal and thus allow DCC-based attenuation map alignment. The approach was evaluated using computer simulated acquisitions of a pinhole cardiac SPECT camera. Two different ECG-gated activity distributions were used. 1) Activity only in the myocardium and 2) activity in both the heart and background structures. ECG-gated projections were fit pixelwise to a sine function to create a sine-amplitude projection. Using exponential DCCs, an attenuation map was translated through a range of spatial positions, and, at each location, the sine-amplitude exponential projection data were evaluated. The attenuation map was aligned where the eDCCs were most consistent, that is, where the relative difference between the eDCC-transformed projections was at a minimum. With myocardium-only activity, using a single gated projection gave a registration error of 0.28 mm, and the sine fit amplitude of ECG-gated projections produced an error of 0.14 mm. With extra-cardiac activity present, the registration error with a single projection was 13.14 mm but reduced to 1.01 mm for the sine amplitude. The sine fit method is a promising approach to correct for the violation of the eDCC-assumptions caused by extra-cardiac activity and thus allow an eDCC-based registration of the attenuation and emission datasets.

articleTitle: Analysis of the Neurological Hallmarks of COVID-19. A Multivariate Approach Using 18F-FDG-PET Data
publicationTitle: 2022 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium and Medical Imaging Conference (NSS/MIC)
abstract: Despite the research efforts put into the study of COVID-19, the long-term neurological implications of this disease are still poorly known. Most studies focus on the description of the symptoms, the treatments applied and the evolution of the patients, but the analysis of the hallmarks caused by COVID-19 in the nervous system is still poorly covered.In this work, we performed a comparative analysis of brain <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">18</sup>F-FDG-PET data from healthy controls and patients who have had COVID-19 and continue to have symptoms and sequelae (Long COVID). By means of a multivariate approach based on the searchlight methodology, we identified some regions with significant differences (p ≤ 0.001) between both groups: Insular lobe, cingulum bundle, supp. motor area and frontal and temporal lobes (among others to a lesser extent). These findings are consistent with previous similar studies, which point to hypoperfusion/hypometabolism in frontal and temporal lobes and nearby areas.

articleTitle: Deep Learning Techniques for Energy Clustering in the CMS Electromagnetic Calorimeter
publicationTitle: 2022 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium and Medical Imaging Conference (NSS/MIC)
abstract: The reconstruction of electrons and photons in CMS is based on topological clustering of the energy they deposit in different crystals of the electromagnetic calorimeter (ECAL). These clusters are built by aggregating neighbouring crystals according to the expected topology of an electromagnetic shower in the ECAL. The presence of upstream material causes electron and photon early showering before reaching the ECAL. This effect, combined with the 3.8 T CMS magnetic field, leads to energy being spread in several clusters around the primary one. It is essential to recover the energy contained in these satellite clusters to achieve the best possible energy resolution. Historically, satellite clusters have been associated to the primary cluster using a purely topological algorithm which does not attempt to remove spurious energy deposits from additional pile-up interactions (PU). The performance of this algorithm is expected to degrade during LHC Run 3 (2022+) because of the larger average PU levels and the increasing levels of noise due to the ageing of the ECAL detector. New methods are being investigated that exploit state-of-the-art deep learning architectures like Graph Neural Networks (GNN) and self-attention algorithms. These more sophisticated models improve the energy collection and are more resilient to PU and noise. This talk will cover the challenges of training the models and the opportunities that this new approach offers.

articleTitle: PET/CT Motion Correction Exploiting Motion Models Fit on Coarsely Gated Data Applied to Finely Gated Data
publicationTitle: 2022 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium and Medical Imaging Conference (NSS/MIC)
abstract: Motion correction is imperative to the reduction of blurring and artefacts inherent in PET; due to the relatively long acquisition time, and the temporal difference in the attenuation map acquisition. Registration literature contains many examples of spatial regularisers, however there are few temporal regularisers. Motion models can act as such a temporal regulariser, as well as allowing for the interpolation of unseen motion correction results. In our previous work, we applied a motion modelling approach to high TOF resolution non-attenuation corrected data; where the data was corrected to the space of the attenuation map. However, this approach was challenging, especially when low contrast lung tumours are present. This work seeks to extend previous work, by incorporating an approach suggested by Y. Lu et al. (JNM 2018), to perform an initial MLACF reconstruction for the motion estimation. In this work, we combine these two approaches, with several improvements, including; µ-map alignment, as well as, fitting the motion model on low noise low temporal/gate resolution data, and applying it to high noise high temporal/gate resolution data. To test this, XCAT volumes are constructed, and TOF data simulated. Evaluation compares the results of the proposed method against, where the motion model was fit on data gated more finely, where the motion model was fit on noiseless data, and finally non-motion corrected examples. Results indicate that the incorporation of MLACF, and fitting of the motion model on low noise low temporal/gate resolution data, improves contrast and quantification, while allowing for a relatively fast execution time.

articleTitle: Standardization of Agnostic Learning Techniques in Neuroimaging: a Case Study in EEG
publicationTitle: 2022 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium and Medical Imaging Conference (NSS/MIC)
abstract: Over the last few years, the use of multivariate pattern analysis (MVPA) has been growing exponentially in cognitive neuroscience. This methodology offers the possibility to perform more detailed studies in electroencephalography (EEG) and other neuroimaging modalities. Usually, machine learning-based algorithms along with empirical out-of sample generalization approaches, e.g. K-fold cross validation (CV), are implemented. In this work we applied a validation approach based on resubstitution with upper bound correction to address the instability problem concerning limited sample sizes, particularly typical in neuroimaging, when estimating accuracy via CV. Moreover, a statistical assessment of the accuracies is conducted. To this end, the methodology underlying Statistical Agnostic Mapping (SAM) to perform spatial detection of regions of interest (ROIs) in neuromaging modalities, such as magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), has been applied to a temporal EEG study. Instead of estimating ROIs by means of a significance maps, the time points where trials are most significant are highlighted. The analyses were implemented on an EEG dataset obtained from 48 participants that performed a simple go-nogo task, in which they were presented names and faces. Here, we classified name and face perception at the subject level. The findings suggest that the use of resubstitution-based approaches can reduce the computational burden and obtain similar, albeit more conservative, results than CV.

articleTitle: Graph-based Analysis of Age-related Changes in the Functional Regions of the Brain using Functional MRI Data
publicationTitle: 2022 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium and Medical Imaging Conference (NSS/MIC)
abstract: Healthy aging is accompanied by a decline in central cognitive abilities. In addition, cognitive decline has been associated with changes in the resting-state functional connectivity patterns of the brain. Therefore, the functional organization of the brain may serve as an optimal tool for designing individualized goal-directed training and therapy for cognitive declined patients. Using the graph theory, we comprehensively investigated these resting-state functional connectivity changes. In this regard, we could address a wide range of questions from the overall topology of the network to the specific functioning of the brain subsystems. We used the resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging data of 24 subjects (age range: 20-71). For each subject, a connectivity matrix is computed based on the Pearson correlation coefficients of average BOLD signals between each pair of brain regions. Then, the average connectivity matrix for each group is calculated to compare the differences in the topology of large-scale networks. The average participation coefficient of each brain network was also computed to accurately determine the topology of changes. Moreover, the network labels were used to find age-related changes in the local connectivity patterns, based on which the average local efficiency of each network was calculated as a measure of local connectivity. Our results suggest that the global efficiency of the brain is highly age-related, exhibiting a significant negative correlation with age. In addition, we found that the segregation of the attentional networks from the default mode network is age-sensitive, which was more specifically explained by the higher participation coefficient of the frontal–parietal control subsystem of the attentional networks, and lower local integration for the default mode, frontal–parietal control, cingulo-opercular control, salience, somatomotor, and auditory networks. To sum up, we provided detailed information to support our hypothesis that healthy aging brings about changes to the function of the dedicated brain regions.

articleTitle: Prompt Gamma Neutron Activation Analysis with Gamma-Gamma Coincidences for Recycling Waste Characterization
publicationTitle: 2022 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium and Medical Imaging Conference (NSS/MIC)
abstract: In the field of circular economy, the detection of strategic elements is required to design and build efficient recycling processes. For instance, the recycling of Waste from Electrical and Electronic Equipment (WEEE) could provide an important supply of several critical elements. Prompt Gamma Neutron Activation Analysis (PGNAA) with a pulsed neutron generator and a high-purity germanium detector (HPGe) allows elemental characterization of bulk samples, but the gamma spectrum includes a large background due to neutron interactions in surrounding materials. Furthermore, the limited HPGe volume only permits a small detection efficiency. The use of large size NaI(Tl) scintillators allows covering wider detection solid angles at reasonable cost, but with a lower energy resolution. In this work, we investigate the use of gamma-gamma coincidences following radiative capture to counterbalance this latter drawback by limiting the neutron-induced gamma ray background. This work describes the implementation of a dedicated PGNAA setup to study gamma-gamma coincidences with a DT pulsed neutron generator and 5"×5"×10" NaI(Tl) scintillators. The setup is optimized with different geometries and shields, such as lead bricks to limit scattering cross talk or B4C sheets to reduce thermal neutron interactions inside the NaI crystals. Optimized data processing also allows rejecting residual cross talk events and random coincidences to maximize the signal/noise ratio.

articleTitle: Time Residual Estimation using Artificial Intelligence
publicationTitle: 2022 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium and Medical Imaging Conference (NSS/MIC)
abstract: A deep-learning based method was implemented to estimate time-residuals (TR) that is performed as part of daily quality control for Biograph Vision 600 high time of flight (TOF) resolution PET/CT scanner. The purpose of this work is to investigate the feasibility of utilizing deep learning to estimate TRs since it is computationally expensive operation due to requirement of non-TOF reconstruction and TOF forward projection and iterative algorithm to estimate TRs. Cylinder scans at 5 different locations were performed to cover the 1 cm radial tolerance from center permitted during positioning of the cylinder. A convolutional neural network with residual connections is utilized. Time-residual ranging from -10 time bins to +10 time bins were simulated to create training, validation, and test data. Time residual error is zero for 38.84% of test crystals, within +/1 time-bins for 87.70 % of test crystals, within +/-2 time-bins for 98.76% of test crystals, within +/-3 time-bins for 99.89, and all the remaining crystals (50 out of 121600) are within +/-7 which is satisfactory for daily QC purposes.

articleTitle: High Bandwidth GPU-Based Data Acquisition for SPECT
publicationTitle: 2022 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium and Medical Imaging Conference (NSS/MIC)
abstract: New generations of SPECT devices will push the limits of current technology to accommodate improvements in detector resolution, increase energy ranges for theranostic radiotracers, and delivering faster results. To accommodate these improvements, data will need to be acquired and processed at rates that were until recently, impossible to achieve. Here we present a prototype system to acquire data over ethernet at rates of up to 200 Gbps and to process in a GPU in real time. We are prototyping using two Nvidia AGX development kits with an RTX 6000 GPU and Mellanox Connect-X6 high bandwidth ethernet NICs. Data is aggregated from multiple 10 Gbps sources using a Mellanox switch to pass data at 100 Gbps to each AGX. In the acquisition machine, data is moved directly from the NIC to the GPU without transferring through the device memory, which increases speed and reduces latency. A comparison will be shown between Nvidia Rivermax and the more conventional GPU-direct RDMA methods of sending data to the GPU. The system is prototyped using an array of development boards that send data packets at a rate of 10 Gbps to emulate a detector output. Multiple data processing methods in the GPU will be presented.

articleTitle: Air Fraction Correction in PET Imaging of Lung Disease – Kernel Determination
publicationTitle: 2022 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium and Medical Imaging Conference (NSS/MIC)
abstract: Accurate quantification of radiotracer uptake from lung PET/CT is challenging due to large variations in fractions of tissue, air, blood, and water. The air fraction correction (AFC) determines voxel-wise air fractions (AF) from the CT acquired for attenuation correction (AC) to correct for the variable air content. However, the resolution mismatch between PET and CT can cause artefacts in the AF-corrected image. In this work, we compare different methodologies for determining the optimal kernel to smooth the CT for AFC, when PET images were reconstructed with iterative reconstruction methods, and in the case where AF-corrected lungs exhibit uniform uptake. Noiseless simulations and non-TOF MLEM reconstructions were performed with STIR via SIRF using a digital test-object constructed from a CT scan of a patient with idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis. The optimal smoothing for AFC was determined via i) the point-source insertion-and-subtraction-method, h<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">pts</inf>; ii) artefact reduction in the AF-corrected volume-of-interest (VOI), h<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">AFC</inf>; iii) smoothing a ground-truth image to match the reconstructed image within the VOI, h<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">PVC</inf>. Each of the three kernels were used to smooth the mu-map for AFC of the reconstructed emission data and the RMSE of each of the AF-corrected VOIs, with respect to the ground-truth, was assessed. Applicability of the preferred method was assessed with phantom acquisitions on a clinical scanner. Results demonstrated that, for iterative reconstruction methods, image resolution is dependent on iteration number and VOI density/uptake. Smoothing by h<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">pts</inf> resulted in the least quantitatively accurate AF-corrected images at fewer than 40 iterations. For both h<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">AFC</inf> and h<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">PVC</inf>, RMSE in the AF-corrected IPF regions is fairly stable across iterations. h<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">PVC</inf> has the potential to be utilised for determining the appropriate kernel for AFC on clinical scanners for application to patient PET/CT lung scans.

articleTitle: Tensor Radiomics: Paradigm for Systematic Incorporation of Multi-Flavoured Radiomics Features
publicationTitle: 2022 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium and Medical Imaging Conference (NSS/MIC)
abstract: Radiomics features extract quantitative information from medical images, towards the derivation of biomarkers for clinical tasks such as diagnosis, prognosis, or treatment response assessment. Different image discretization parameters (e.g. bin number or size), convolutional filters, segmentation perturbation, or multi-modality fusion levels can be used to generate radiomics features and ultimately signatures. Commonly, only one set of parameters is used, resulting in only one value or ‘flavour’ for a given feature. We propose ‘tensor radiomics’ (TR) where tensors of features calculated with multiple combinations of parameters (i.e. flavours) are utilized to optimize the construction of radiomics signatures. We have applied TR to PET/CT, MRI, and CT imaging, invoking machine learning or deep learning solutions, and reproducibility analyses. Given space limitations, here we present example results on PET/CT imaging: (1) TR via varying bin sizes on PET-CT images of head & neck cancer (HNC) for overall survival prediction. A hybrid deep neural network, referred to as ‘TR-Net’, along with two ML-based flavour fusion methods showed improved accuracy compared to regular radiomics features; and (2) TR via multiple PET/CT fusions in HNC: flavours were built from different fusions using methods such as Laplacian pyramids and wavelet transforms. We also tried TR based on segmentation perturbation flavours and preprocessing-filter flavours in CT and MR images. TR showed improved reproducibility as well as overall survival prediction compared to single-flavoured radiomics. Our results suggest that the proposed TR paradigm has the potential to improve performance capabilities in different medical imaging tasks.

articleTitle: Front-End Electronics Development for a Fine Pitch AC Coupled Double-Sided LiInSe2 Strip Detector
publicationTitle: 2022 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium and Medical Imaging Conference (NSS/MIC)
abstract: This paper describes the development of a fine pitch AC coupled double-sided strip LiInSe<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> neutron imaging detector for DOE user facilities. The detector being developed is targeting a high spatial resolution as low as 5 µm and a timing resolution of less than 1 µs. To reach our objectives and challenges, a double-sided cross-strip configuration is considered with a fine strip pitch as small as 40 µm patterned on a LiInSe<inf xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</inf> substrate and coupled to our detection system. The large amount of data expected to be collected per each strip required the development of a specific and suitable readout system, which is described in this paper. This detection system is built based on front-end electronics consisting of four VATAGP7 ASICs placed on a custom daughter board that is in turn connected to an already developed main acquisition board for readout process control.

articleTitle: Simulation of Charge Collection in a Boron-coated Straw Detector for Emerging Fuel Cycles
publicationTitle: 2022 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium and Medical Imaging Conference (NSS/MIC)
abstract: Tristructural-isotropic (TRISO) fuel is currently one of the most mature fuel types for candidate advanced reactor types, namely pebble bed reactors (PBRs). In PBRs, TRISO- fueled pebbles can be re-introduced into the core several times before reaching their target bumup. Non-destructive techniques capable of assaying <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">235</sup>U mass in the pebble are therefore needed for nuclear material control and accountability during fuel recirculation. In this work, we have developed a new boron- coated straw (BCS) based neutron multiplicity counter (NMC) to estimate <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">236</sup>U mass in each pebble. BCS detectors are chosen for their inherent high insensitivity to gamma rays that will enable their use to assay also irradiated pebbles and high neutron detection efficiency, comparable to <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">3</sup>He detectors. The BCS- based NMC that we have designed was built by Proportional Technologies, Inc. (PTI) Houston, TX. In this work, we report the system-level simulation of the BCS-based NMC and the straw- level charge collection simulation coupled with a custom software to tally the detected pulse integral from the list mode energy deposited. We have developed a high-fidelity model of the NMC to simulate the response of a single straw detector to a <sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">262</sup>Cf source. The simulated die-away time, single neutron count rate, and double neutron count rate agree well with measured values, with a relative difference within ±0.4%. The simulated charge spectrum agrees well with the measured one in the case of a round straw. We plan to use the NMC to perform active and passive interrogation of fresh and spent fuel pebbles.

articleTitle: Study of a Dynamically Reconfigurable Data Readout Scheme of a Pixel Readout ASIC for Hybrid X-ray Imaging Detectors
publicationTitle: 2022 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium and Medical Imaging Conference (NSS/MIC)
abstract: The application of hybrid pixel detectors with a dynamically selectable readout mode in X-ray imaging is highly desirable. The concept of a detector system that can switch readout mode under different conditions is demanded to realize fast and versatile imaging. This paper presents design techniques and preliminary results of a pixel readout ASIC prototype with a reconfigurable readout scheme in a 180 nm CMOS process for silicon pixel detectors. A bus-based reconfigurable data readout scheme is presented. Three readout modes are realized: full-frame readout, zero-suppression readout, and region-of-interest readout. In particular application scenarios, the readout mode will be switched based on the number of pixels with valid data to improve the frame rate. Assuming that all pixels with valid data are transmitted, the reconfigurable data readout method saves 40 % of the data transmission time than zero-suppression readout under 50 MHz.

articleTitle: Supervised Classification of Mean Diffusivity in Substantia Nigra for Parkinson's Disease Diagnosis
publicationTitle: 2022 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium and Medical Imaging Conference (NSS/MIC)
abstract: The substantia nigra (SN) is one of the brain regions commonly affected by neurodegenerative diseases, including Parkinson's disease (PD). The neurodegenerative process could be characterized through diffusion tensor imaging (DTI). Recent DTI studies corroborated this assumption that significantly lower fractional anisotropy (FA) and higher mean diffusivity (MD) values are observed in the SN in patients with PD compared to healthy control (HC) subjects. Since the accuracy of diagnosis based on clinical criteria is low, an automated learning-based method such as a support vector machine (SVM) is required to diagnose the disease based on FA and MD signal alternation. The aim of this study was to optimize and compare five commonly used classifications methods, including K-nearest neighbor (KNN), support vector machine (SVM), tree classification, Naïve Bayes, and ensemble classifiers to find the best technique to discriminate early PD from HC based on MD values in the SN. K-nearest neighbor (KNN) and Ensemble classifier outperformed other classification methods in the diagnosis of PD with 81%, 78% accuracy, and 78%, 82% sensitivity, respectively. Our results showed that although SVM in most cases exhibited good performance in classifying PD patients based on DTI data, for classification of the PD and HC based on the MD values of left and right SN, KNN performed better. In this regard, the Ensemble method with an AUC of 75% exhibited superior performance to SVM.

articleTitle: Assessment of Gaussian and Multi-gaussian Kernel Models for the Reconstruction of TOF-PET Datasets with Event-by-Event Variable Time Resolution
publicationTitle: 2022 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium and Medical Imaging Conference (NSS/MIC)
abstract: Most current TOF-PET systems uses a global TOF uncertainty model during image reconstruction. Image artifacts can appear if the kernel model differs to much from the actual TOF kernel width, in particular when time resolution improves. Additionally, new detector designs such as hybrid Cherenkov/scintillation systems, detectors based on meta-materials in which different events can have a very different timing resolution, or 3 gamma imaging system bring several challenges as the TOF uncertainty model should be adapted in order to take advantage of the information carried by each detected event. This work focuses on (1) evaluating with Monte-Carlo simulated datasets a previously proposed analytical approach to estimate the SNR gain from a dataset with variable time resolution, and (2) study the performance of the use of different TOF kernel models for the reconstuction of datasets containing events with variable TOF information.Several datasets containing events ranging from 400 to 30 ps CRT were generated to produce 100 noise realizations. From these datasets, several mixes of labeled and unlabeled events were created, to generate datasets with either events with an unique CRT, or various mixes of events with different CRT. These datasets were then reconstructed using a gaussian TOF uncertainty model, as well as a weighed sum of gaussians. An image of pixel variances was computed for each approach from the set of 100 reconstructed images in order to derive SNR gain values.The evaluated analytical estimation approach was validated with these simulated results, both for datasets containing events with the same CRT or various mixes of different CRT. The use of a sum of gaussian provided a slightly better SNR when there is an acute difference in the proportion of events composing a mixed dataset, although this increase was not significant suggesting than using one gaussian model is still a reasonable approximation for these datasets.Future work will focus on the study of the different models with more realistic simulated datasets and ultra-fast time resolution.

articleTitle: Development of a Digital Brain Phantom Population for Radionuclide Imaging Research in Parkinson’s Disease
publicationTitle: 2022 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium and Medical Imaging Conference (NSS/MIC)
abstract: Parkinson’s disease (PD) can be early diagnosed using radionuclide imaging. Digital phantoms and Monte Carlo (MC) simulations serve as important research tools for PD imaging physics research. Here we designed and developed a new digital brain phantom population for different stages of PD. We selected 206 T1 MRI brain images and 160 DaTscan SPECT reconstructed images for normal subjects and patients with different PD stages from Parkinson’s Progression Markers Initiative (PPMI) datasets. We used the model-based segmentation tool FIRST to segment putamen and caudate region and used Brain Extraction Tool (BET) to extract brain region from the MRI images, generating striatum and brain maps, respectively. Striatum maps were then rigidly registered to a referenced striatum model using Elastix, and the corresponding brain maps were transformed using the same parameters. Different activities were set on the maps based on the striatal binding ratio (SBR) in PPMI and the SPECT Visual interpretation assessment scheme. New phantoms were generated by randomly pairing the striatum and brain maps. Corresponding CT maps were generated by non-rigidly registered the XCAT-attenuation map to MRI images corresponding to the brain maps and transformed using the same parameters. We then used the Simind MC code to generate 120 realistic noisy projections with full physics modelling for each new brain phantom, based on a clinical SPECT scanner mounted with low-energy high-resolution parallel-hole collimators. OS-EM algorithm (8 iterations, 4 subsets) was used to reconstruct projections with and without attenuation correction (AC) respectively. SBR was evaluated on reconstructed images. Our results show that we could generate realistic PD SPECT data with the newly developed digital brain phantom population combined with a MC code, and AC is important for PD SPECT based on both visual assessment and SBR analysis. Our phantoms could be applied for further PD radionuclide imaging study.

articleTitle: Automated Pulmonary Nodule Detection from Different Levels of Low Dose CT Images using 3D Convolutional Networks
publicationTitle: 2022 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium and Medical Imaging Conference (NSS/MIC)
abstract: There are several techniques to diagnose lung cancer, wherein recently low dose CT imaging has attracted much attention. Early diagnosis of lung cancer can improve the chance of curing this disease. In this light, the goal of this work is to develop deep learning-based algorithms to identify the lung lesions from low-dose CT images (classifying the lung nodules into cancerous and benign). To this end, the lung nodule analysis 2016 challenge (LUNA 16) dataset was employed in this study. Different low-dose CT images including 10%, 20%, 40%, and 60% of the full-dose (reference) CT scan were generated/simulated. We trained a convolutional network with full-dose and low-dose CT images. In the first evaluation phase, low-dose CT images (at different dose levels) were fed to the model trained with full-dose CT data. The results of this phase were reported separately. Then, the low-dose CT images were processed with the corresponding models trained with the same low-dose data. The results of this validation phase were compared with those of the first phase. The validation was carried out using 400 cancerous and 400 benign nodes randomly fed into the different models. Even though the full dose model achieved an accuracy of 97% when evaluated using the full-dose CT data, this model exhibited suboptimal/poor performance when low-dose CT data were used as input. When the convolutional models were trained and evaluated with the same low dose CT, the accuracy of the malignant node detection was dramatically improved. The accuracy of the node detection dropped from 97% to 60% when the 10% low dose CT data was fed into the full-dose model, while the dedicated model for 10% low-dose CT data achieved an accuracy of 90%. The model trained on the full dose CT data exhibited very poor accuracy while the dedicated models developed for each low-dose level led to an acceptable accuracy.

articleTitle: An FPGA Based Sub-Nanosecond Hit Time Measurement Board for the Muon Spectrometer of the ATLAS Experiment at HL-LHC
publicationTitle: 2022 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium and Medical Imaging Conference (NSS/MIC)
abstract: The first level hardware muon trigger system in the barrel region of the ATLAS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) at CERN selects muon candidates with predefined transverse momentum and tags them with their Bunch Crossing number and geometrical coordinates. Four concentric layers of Resistive Plate Chambers (RPC) will be used as muon trigger detectors in the barrel region of the experiment for the Run4 of the High Luminosity LHC (HL-LHC), starting in 2029. The first level hardware muon trigger system for Run4 selects muon candidates using a coincidence-based algorithm on the four RPC layers. The usage of FPGA devices for both on-detector and off-detector trigger electronics is an ideal choice since it allows to take advantage of the FPGA increasing resources, performances, flexibility and radiation tolerance. The Data Collector and Transmitter (DCT) board will be used to readout the RPC detector. This board digitises up to 288 RPC front-end hit signals and measures the hit time of arrival with respect to the LHC 40 MHz bunch crossing clock. The DCT FPGA firmware implements a sub-nanosecond Time-to-Digital-Converter (TDC) used to time tag the incoming hit data. The TDC data are zero-suppressed to minimise the output bandwidth and then serially sent out to the barrel muon trigger off-detector electronics through optical fibres. The off-detector electronics execute the first level muon trigger algorithm and the RPC detector readout logic.

Author Keywords: This paper describes the DCT boar
its firmware and its tested performances

articleTitle: Characterisation of the Upgraded MERMAID Prototype, a PET/CT Device for Small Aquatic Animals
publicationTitle: 2022 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium and Medical Imaging Conference (NSS/MIC)
abstract: Zebrafish and other small aquatic animals are model organisms used to study human diseases. To extend Positron Emission Tomography (PET) to such small animals, dedicated concepts are necessary. We are developing Multi-Emission Radioisotopes - Marine Animal Imaging Device (MERMAID), the first prototype conceived for radioisotope imaging of small aquatic animals. A first characterization of the new modules shows a homogeneous behavior of the individual channels. Furthermore, a linear response was determined for activities from approx. 1 to 5 MBq. Further characterization and and image quality measurements are to be carried out.

articleTitle: Enhancing 3D Gamma-Ray Imaging with Through-Wall Radar
publicationTitle: 2022 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium and Medical Imaging Conference (NSS/MIC)
abstract: Detecting, localizing, and quantifying concealed nuclear material is a problem relevant to locating sources outside of regulatory control, containing contamination, and preventing illegal transport of radioactive materials. Recent advances include the ability to locate and quantify point sources in 3D more accurately by taking into account the attenuating materials between the source and a gamma-ray detector and by obtaining scene information through LiDAR measurements. These efforts have greatly improved the localization and quantification of obstructed sources, but they neglect internal structure composed of gamma-ray attenuating materials that LiDAR cannot detect. In this work, we report upon model-based efforts to advance the state-of-the-art by exploring the increased performance in quantitative gamma-ray imaging through the use of Through-Wall Radar Imaging (TWRI) to gain more information about the scene.

articleTitle: Feasibility Study of an Integrated Prompt Gamma Imaging and PET System for Range Verification in Proton Therapy
publicationTitle: 2022 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium and Medical Imaging Conference (NSS/MIC)
abstract: Proton range verification in vivo is beneficial and significant for precision treatment in proton therapy. Prompt gamma imaging (PGI) and positron emission tomography (PET) are two potential methods for in vivo range verification by measuring secondary particles produced in proton therapy. In this work we proposed an integrated prompt gamma and positron emission imaging system based on all-digital PET panel detectors and have performed Monte Carlo simulations to investigate the feasibility. The system consists of two panel PET detectors and collimators. During proton beam irradiation, prompt gamma one dimensional imaging could be performed by panel detectors combined with collimators. After proton beam irradiation, the collimators are moved and then positron emission imaging will be performed. This system could perform PGI and PET in one therapy fraction, which is able to increase the adaptability of the system for proton range verification in different treatment scenarios. On the other hand, it promises to achieve more accurate range verification by combining PGI and PET.

articleTitle: A Low-Noise Readout Channel for X-Ray Ptychography Applications
publicationTitle: 2022 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium and Medical Imaging Conference (NSS/MIC)
abstract: In the present work, the design of a readout channel for a pixelated detector to be employed in X-ray ptychography is proposed and discussed. The channel is developed in a commercial 65 nm CMOS technology, features single photon detection at 5 keV, 9 keV, and 25 keV photons, with a noise of 250 e<sup xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">-</sup> rms, a power consumption of 220 µW, and fits in an area of 150 µm × 150 µm. The readout channel is the elementary cell of an envisioned 128-by-128 pixel matrix and it is designed for operation at a 1 MHz conversion rate. A prototype 8-by-2 matrix, included in the pFREYA16 ASIC, was submitted to foundry to prove the feasibility of such detector. Preliminary noise evaluations, design considerations and post-layout simulation of a single pixel will be presented in this paper.

articleTitle: CMOS SPADs for High Radiation Environments
publicationTitle: 2022 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium and Medical Imaging Conference (NSS/MIC)
abstract: We first characterized large 180 nm CMOS single-photon avalanche diode (SPAD) imagers under 10 and 100 MeV protons irradiation up to a displacement damage dose of 1 PeV/g. We used the dark count rate (DCR) to assess the non-ionizing damage levels created by protons. It is shown that the DCR levels are determined by the number and the type of defects created within the photocollector region of the irradiated SPAD. It is also found that the activation energies correspond to the defect energy levels of oxygen-vacancy, divacancy, and phosphorus-vacancy complexes. After irradiation, a DCR reduction was observed under room temperature, which shows the transient response of DCR induced by ionizing damage. Furthermore, high-temperature annealing was performed to accelerate recovery. We then measured the timing performance of individual SPADs with photons and 180 GeV/c pions employed as minimum ionizing particles (MIP). Both results showed sub-10 ps timing resolution per single detector. Overall, the devices under test retain reasonable DCR after the high dose of radiation, showing SPADs have the potential to be used in long-term space missions or high energy physics applications.

articleTitle: Estimation of Electron Density from joint Reconstructions of Activity and Attenuation of ToF-PET Scans for Particle Therapy
publicationTitle: 2022 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium and Medical Imaging Conference (NSS/MIC)
abstract: The aim of the study is to provide a novel type of computed tomography (CT) image set for the dose calculation in particle therapy. These gamma-ray attenuation images (γCTs) are derived from time-of-flight PET (ToF-PET) scans utilizing the joint reconstruction of activity and attenuation, particularly the Maximum Likelihood estimation of Attenuation and Activity (MLAA). As the γCTs are established from 511 keV photons, there is an inherent linearity of the attenuation values of the voxels and the electron density. The latter is the most important material characteristics, which determines the slowing down of particles in matter. A phantom was built, which mimics the lower part of a human head. Inserts of varying electron density were immersed in FDG filled water solution within a cylindrical container. The grayscale levels of the reconstructed images were analyzed and compared with the material specification provided by the vendors of the inserts. A model to convert the material properties from the CT numbers was developed. The data from the images were in agreement with a linear model. In future investigations, the influence on the reduction of uncertainties in proton therapy treatment planning will be derived from the results.

articleTitle: Deep-Learning Based Super-Resolution for Low-Dose CT
publicationTitle: 2022 IEEE Nuclear Science Symposium and Medical Imaging Conference (NSS/MIC)
abstract: Recently we proposed a texture transformer network for the image super-resolution (TTSR), a reference-based deep learning super-resolution method, to improve the spatial resolution and suppress the noise of computed tomography (CT) images, where its effectiveness was demonstrated using the XCAT phantom. In this work, we focus on developing TTSR for real patient CT data. The mapping from the noisy low-resolution CT (LRCT) images to the clean high-resolution CT (HRCT) images is learned through TTSR. First, we iteratively reconstruct HRCT (full-dose, full projection data, 512x512 image resolution) and LRCT (quarter dose, 1/4 of all projection data, 128x128 image resolution) images using the CT projection data from 10 patients. Then, the TTSR models are trained using LRCT and HRCT images from nine patients to establish the translation from LRCT images to HRCT images.
